C I T 3 Theoretical background and hypothesis develop- R A ment As systemic risk, which is distinct from individual risks, typically manifests as a system-wide phenomenon, it is often accompanied by synchronized movements within the financial sector (Allen and Carletti 2013; Benoit et al., 2017). For instance, when a risk factor impacts multiple financial institutions concurrently, it can trigger extensive losses across the system, potentially leading to a systemic crisis. Thus, the homogeneity of the corporate risk perception has the potential to signify systemic risk. In a financial system, the homogeneity of risk perceptions among financial institu- tions can be theoretically linked to systemic risk through two distinct mechanisms. For one thing, greater homogeneity in risk perceptions among financial institutions may stem from their extensive business operations and large scale. Such breadth and depth often lead to a more holistic approach to risk management, encompassing a wider range of potential risks. This is in line with the too-big-to-fail theory (Mishkin, 2006), which posits that a crisis involving a large and influential institution can escalate into systemic 4 ARTICLE IN PRESS financial risk, given its critical role in the financial network. For another, the higher the homogeneity of risks perceived by financial institutions, the more probable it becomes to encounter shared shocks across the system. Common shocks can swiftly propagate through the financial system, disproportionately affecting institutions with similar risk profiles. This shared vulnerability aligns with the concept of herding behavior, where institutions, due to analogous risk assessments or correlated exposures, face synchronized impacts during periods of stress. As the shocks cascade, a domino effect may emerge, triggering widespread failures among interdependent institutions and destabilizing the financial system as a whole. The homogeneity in risk perception could signal a form of financial connectedness that might affect systemic risk. Thus, we propose the first hypothesis: Hypothesis 1: Reflecting financial connectedness in the dimension of risk percep- tion, higher homogeneity in the risk perception of financial institutions could be informa- S tive for an increase in systemic risk. Both P types of factors can cause the contagion am ong the financial institutions, generating N turmoil in the system. In our situation, the risk perceptions among the institutions are I differentiated,sothatitisnoteasyforal ltheinstitutionstosimultaneouslydiscloseallthe E global factors they confront. Thus, we categorize the risks into general and specific ones. L The former reflects the risks identified by the majority of financial institutions, whereas C the latter signifies risks that are particular to a few institutions. The higher homogeneity I T of corporate risk perception associated with general risks (i.e., common risks prevalent in R the financial market) means that more financial institutions are simultaneously exposed A to these kinds of risks. This could increase systemic risk by amplifying synchronized institutional exposure to common shocks in the entire financial system. Specific risks (i.e., heterogeneous risks faced by specific institutions or sectors) may not be as prevalent in number as general risks. However, the great connectivity associated with these specific risks indicates that these risks are highly concentrated among specific institutions or sectors. The aggregated risks faced by these institutions or sectors potentially lead to system-wide losses as well, through intensified vulnerability at critical network nodes. To this end, we develop the second hypothesis: Hypothesis 2a: Greater homogeneity in perceptions of general risks, which are systemically prevalent across financial institutions, is associated with higher levels of sys- temic risk. Hypothesis 2b: Greater homogeneity in perceptions of specific risks, which are concentrated within particular institutions, is also associated with higher levels of systemic risk. However, from the perspective of reaction to the risks, the increased homogeneity in risk perception among corporations can foster better coordination in responding to crises. According to coordination theory (Malone, 1987), when firms share similar risk perceptions, they are more likely to align their actions in a way that reduces the potential for disruptive behaviors, such as excessive risk-taking or panic selling. This coordinated response is essential during financial crises, as it allows institutions to take preemptive and collective measures—such as conserving liquidity, deleveraging, or adhering to regulatory guidelines—that can stabilize the financial sys- tem. The concept of common knowledge from game theory (Brandenburger, 1992) also supports this view because it emphasizes the idea that when all players (in this case, financial institutions) have a shared understanding of a particular situation, their actions become more predictable and coordinated. In a crisis, where uncertainty is high, having a common understanding of the risks at play ensures that institutions make decisions S that are aligned with one another. JSON: Name: risk_perception_homogeneity_sysrisk Title: Measuring the effect of corporate risk-perception homogeneity derived from 10-K risk-factor text on systemic financial risk using sent-LDA and network centrality Short Hypothesis: Greater homogeneity in corporate risk perceptions across financial institutions causes an increase in systemic financial risk as measured by SRISK and MES. Related Work: Existing approaches to quantify systemic financial risk rely on observed balance-sheet linkages, interbank liabilities, overlapping-portfolio similarity, asset return co-movements, and institution-level systemic risk indices. Separately, textual analyses of corporate filings have been used to extract firm-specific risk factors and to predict firm outcomes, but they are typically applied at the micro level. Prior network-based work infers interconnectedness from explicit exposures, portfolio overlaps, or market co-movement, which can miss forward-looking or non-financial exposures. Limitations in current methods include reliance on structured financial data that omit unobserved shared exposures, coarse-grained co-movement measures that conflate correlation with exposure, and text approaches that extract topics but do not aggregate them into a network measure of homogeneity or separate general versus idiosyncratic risk-types. Causal inference between interconnectedness and systemic risk remains weak in prior work due to endogeneity and limited tests of crisis-period interactions. Abstract: We propose a reproducible research pipeline that quantifies corporate risk-perception homogeneity from mandated 10-K risk-factor text and evaluates its causal association with systemic financial risk. The pipeline extracts sentence-level topics from risk-factor headings using a sentence-aware topic model to produce firm-level risk-type frequency vectors. Pairwise cosine similarity of those vectors creates an annual similarity network whose node centralities define firm-level homogeneity measures. We test whether increases in homogeneity predict higher systemic risk (SRISK and MES) using panel regressions with firm and year fixed effects, Granger-causality tests, and crisis-period interaction models. The main contribution is a validated, text-driven channel for measuring forward-looking interconnectedness and demonstrating that homogeneity in perceived risks is predictive of systemic risk while exhibiting different behavior in crisis versus non-crisis periods. Expected outcomes include quantified effect sizes, robustness across alternative text and network constructions, and evaluation of general versus specific risk-types. Experiments: Datasets: (1) EDGAR 10-K filings risk-factor headings for all U.S. listed financial institutions (2006–2020) aggregated per fiscal year (approx. 538,269 headings); (2) CRSP daily stock returns (same sample period) to compute MES and input for SRISK; (3) Compustat annual balance-sheet variables for controls (size, leverage, ROA, net working capital). Baselines: (A) network from overlapping portfolio similarity (asset-holdings cosine similarity); (B) network from return co-movements (rolling correlation threshold network); (C) explicit interbank exposures where available; (D) text baseline using standard LDA topic vectors; (E) random network null. Text processing and feature extraction: sentence-aware topic model (sent-LDA) to infer N topics (select N by coherence and stability), map topics to labeled risk-types, build firm-year normalized risk-type frequency vectors. Network construction: pairwise cosine similarity matrix per year; construct weighted networks and compute node measures: weighted degree centrality (NH), closeness, eigenvector centrality. Systemic risk measures: compute daily MES and SRISK per firm, aggregate to annual firm-level dependent variables (annual mean). Main tests: panel regressions of SRISK and MES on lagged homogeneity measures with firm and year fixed effects and controls; Granger causality panel tests for directionality. Comparisons and ablations: (1) sent-LDA vs LDA topic extraction; (2) headings-only vs full risk-section text; (3) cosine similarity vs Jaccard and TF-IDF cosine; (4) thresholded binary network vs weighted network; (5) partitioned regressions for general (top 30% disclosed topics) vs specific risks; (6) crisis interaction models (dummy for 2008–2010 and 2020). Evaluation metrics: regression coefficient sign and significance (p-values), effect sizes, adjusted R-squared, AIC/BIC, Granger causality p-values, out-of-sample predictive RMSE for year-ahead aggregate systemic risk, topic coherence scores, network stability via bootstrap (confidence intervals for node centralities). Implementation and setup: preprocess filings (normalize headings, remove boilerplate, lemmatize), tune sent-LDA hyperparameters via held-out likelihood and coherence, normalize vectors by firm-year total headings, compute annual networks, run regressions with clustered standard errors at firm level, perform robustness checks across alternative topic counts and similarity measures, and report full model diagnostics and sensitivity analyses. Risk Factors and Limitations: Technical failure modes: poor topic extraction quality due to short or boilerplate headings can produce noisy risk-type vectors and false similarity links; heterogeneous filing formats and OCR errors may bias extraction. Data and evaluation biases: sample restricted to U.S. listed financial firms introduces selection and survivorship bias and limits generalizability to unlisted or non-U.S. institutions; SRISK and MES are model-based constructs subject to measurement error and may reflect market sentiment rather than fundamentals. Causal identification limits: panel regressions and Granger tests cannot fully rule out omitted variable confounding or reverse causality (systemic risk could drive disclosure homogeneity); endogeneity from concurrent regulatory changes or macro shocks. Scalability and compute: sentence-level topic modeling on hundreds of thousands of headings requires nontrivial compute and memory; network computations and bootstrap stability analyses increase runtime. Sensitivity to design choices: results depend on topic count, topic labeling, similarity metric, and thresholding for network edges; choices may change estimated effect sizes. Limits to generalization: disclosure regimes, language, and risk vocabulary evolve over time and across jurisdictions, so the pipeline's transferability to other countries or later periods is constrained.
